title: The Divan
hook: Rumi's collected lyric poems, many signed with the name of his friend Shams
tomorrow: Rumi says he died as a mineral. what could he possibly mean?

segments.voice: Yesterday the reading closed with the good guest's sentence: thank the hosts. Now a new stretch of days, the poets as companions, and the first poet signs the wrong name.

Some songwriters make a whole album about one person, and you can hear the name between the lines. Rumi went further. His collected lyric poems are called a divan, and Reynold Nicholson's old English selection is titled after the Divan of Shams of Tabriz. Shams, not Rumi. Many of the poems close by naming Shams. So, today's question: why would a poet put another man's name on his own poems?
screen: `AN ALBUM ABOUT ONE PERSON.` → `THE DIVAN OF SHAMS OF TABRIZ.` → `WHY ANOTHER MAN'S NAME?`

segments.voice: The story, as tradition tells it: Rumi was a respected scholar and preacher in Konya when a wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, came to town. The two became inseparable, so much that Rumi's students grew jealous. Then Shams was gone. Out of that loss came a flood of poems, and where a poet would set his own name, Rumi set his friend's. Here's the answer, from inside Rumi's own world. In Sufi Islam, love for a spiritual friend can become a road to the love of God, and on that road the self steps aside. Sufis call that passing away of the self fana. Signing as Shams is a poet saying: this voice isn't only mine. Now the unity thread. Sikh scripture holds something close. Hymns by the later Gurus in the Guru Granth Sahib are signed with one name, Nanak, the first Guru. In the Sikh telling, one light passed from Guru to Guru, so the name stays the same. Shared: a poet hiding his own name inside a beloved teacher's. The honest difference: for Sikhs those hymns are scripture, sung before the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru; for Muslims, Rumi's divan is treasured poetry, not scripture, and Shams was a friend, not a successor. One to tell a friend tonight: even in Persian, Rumi's great collection of lyric poems goes by his friend's name, the Divan of Shams.
screen: `SHAMS COMES TO KONYA.` · `THEN SHAMS IS GONE.` · `FANA: THE SELF STEPS ASIDE.` · `THE GURUS SIGN AS NANAK.` · then, large: `THE DIVAN.`

segments.voice: Open any poem you love, by Rumi if you have one, and read it aloud slowly, letting your voice carry it all the way to the last line. At the end, notice whose name, or whose face, the poem leaves you with.
Divan: a poet's collected poems. Rumi's is known by his friend's name, the Divan of Shams of Tabriz.
Here's the line: the divan, a book of love poems signed with a friend's name. Until tomorrow.
